questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_130-->If most résumés are about selling yourself for the ideal career opportunity, why should they not include any personal data? Why should employers not insist on a résumé with the applicant's picture on it but welcome video résumés?

generalfeedback.text:
(Answers may vary.) A candidate should be recruited when his or her qualifications and work-experience meet the needs of the position and the organization. However, the following factors are not suitable criteria for recruiting a candidate and result in employers facing a complaint of discriminatory hiring practices: physical characteristics, age, gender, marital status, sexual orientation, religious or political affiliations, race, national origin, salary history, reasons for leaving jobs, names of previous supervisors, names of references, Social Security number, or student ID number.
Employers should not insist on a résumé with the applicant's picture on it because it could amount to discrimination based on physical characteristics. The picture can also provide visual cues about age, ethnicity, and gender. Organizations are expected to evaluate candidates solely on the basis of their credentials. Video résumés should only be considered as a supplement. To make the hiring process more transparent and faster, most organizations do not welcome video résumés.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_131-->Is the format of your résumé a criterion for an employer to judge your compatibility with their organization? Explain your answer. As a potential employer, what résumé formats would you encourage and why?

generalfeedback.text:
(Answers may vary.) The format of a résumé is one of the criteria employers use to judge an applicant's compatibility with their organization. If the résumé is not in the format the employer specified-such as plain-text files, PDF files, or online résumés-it might indicate the applicant's inability to follow instructions and preferences and might not even be considered. By insisting that a résumé be sent in a particular format, especially online, the employer might also be judging the applicant's knowledge of media and technology.
Students can choose from various résumé formats, such as PDF files, online résumés, and traditional printed résumés. They should explain the reasons for their choice, such as how nontraditional formats like online résumés can be easily processed and are paperless.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_132-->Describe the six most common formats in which you can produce a résumé. What are some other kinds of formats? When and how should they be used?

generalfeedback.text:
A printed résumé should be brought to the interview, even if you applied online. The résumé can serve as a note-taking form or discussion guide, and it is tangible evidence of your attention to professionalism and detail. When printing a résumé, choose a heavier, higher-quality paper. White or slightly off-white is the best color choice. Avoid papers with borders or backgrounds.
A scannable résumé differs from the traditional format in two major ways: it should always include a keyword summary (employers search on these terms to find promising candidates), and it should be formatted in a simpler fashion that avoids underlining, special characters, and other elements that can confuse the scanning system.
A plain-text file (sometimes known as an ASCII text file) is an electronic version of your résumé that has no font formatting, no bullet symbols, no colours, no lines or boxes, or other formatting.
A Microsoft Word document preserves the design and layout of your résumé and saves you the trouble of creating a plain-text version.
Creating a PDF file is a simple procedure, but you need the right software. Adobe Acrobat (not the free Adobe Reader) is the best-known program, but many others are available, including some free versions.
Online résumés provide the opportunity to expand on the information contained in your basic résumé with links to projects, publications, screencasts, online videos, course lists, social  networking profiles, and other elements that give employers a more complete picture of you.
In addition to these six main formats, some applicants create PowerPoint presentations, videos, or infographics to supplement a conventional résumé. These formats should complement a conventional résumé, not replace it.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_140-->________ is the most important website to incorporate into your job search.
Discuss nine tips for creating a successful LinkedIn profile.

generalfeedback.text:
1. Photo. Add a photo that says "professional" without being overly formal. You don't need to hire a professional photographer, but the photo needs to be clear and lit well enough so that your face isn't in shadow. Stand against a visually "quiet" background that won't distract viewers, dress appropriately for the jobs you are pursuing, and remember to smile. A "head and shoulders" photo is most common.
  2. Headline. Write a headline that expresses who you are or aspire to be as a professional, such as "Data science major ready to make data come alive through leading-edge techniques in data mining, visualization, and AI." Include keywords that target employers are likely to be searching for. Like other text fields on LinkedIn, you have a limited number of characters to work with, so focus on your most valuable attributes.
  3. Summary. Write a summary that captures where you are and where you are going. Imagine that you are talking to a hiring manager in a personal and conversational tone, telling the story of where you've been and where you would like to go-but expressed in terms of meeting an employer's business needs. Highlight your job experience, education, skills, accomplishments, target industry, and career direction. Unlike the introductory statement on your conventional résumé, which you can fine-tune for every job opportunity, your LinkedIn summary offers a more general picture of who you are as a professional. Be sure to work in as many of the keywords from your research as you can, while keeping the style natural. Employers can use a variety of search tools to find candidates, and they'll look for these keywords.
  4. Experience. Fill out the experience section, using the material from your conventional résumé. Make sure the details of your employment match your résumé, as employers are likely to cross-check. However, you can expand beyond those basics, including linking to photos and videos of work-related accomplishments.
  5. Recommendations. Ask for recommendations from people you know on LinkedIn. You may have a limited number of connections as you start out, but as your network expands you'll have more people to ask. A great way to get recommendations is to give them to the people in your network.
  6. Featured skills. List your top skills and areas of expertise. As you expand your network, endorse the skills of people you know; many users will endorse your skills in return.
  7. Education. Make sure your educational listing is complete and matches the information on your conventional résumé.
  8. Accomplishments. LinkedIn offers a variety of categories that let you highlight academic achievements, special projects, publications, professional certifications, important coursework, honours, patents, and more. If you don't have an extensive work history, use this section to feature academic projects and other accomplishments that demonstrate your skills.
  9. Volunteer experience and causes. Add volunteering activities and charitable organizations that you support.

<!--RsQ_022-->Explain the importance of networking as part of your career search, and describe how to find helpful networks.

generalfeedback.text: Networking is the process of making informal connections with a broad sphere of mutually beneficial business contacts. Research suggests that it is currently the most common way that employees find jobs. Helpful networks are available in person and online. You can find them by reading news sites, blogs, and other online sources, by participating in student business organizations, and by visiting trade shows that cater to the industry you're interested in. Volunteering in social, civic, and religious organizations can also help you create a network for yourself.

<!--RsQ_053-->List and describe the three methods for organizing a résumé along with their advantages and disadvantages.

generalfeedback.text: 1. Chronological-lists your employment history starting with the most recent job first. Advantages include: employers are familiar with it, it highlights growth and career progression, and it emphasizes continuity and stability. Disadvantages: it draws attention to gaps in your employment history. 2. Functional-lists your skills and accomplishments. Advantages include: employers can quickly see what you can do, you can emphasize earlier job experience, and de-emphasize any lack of career progress or lengthy unemployment. Disadvantages: employers tend to assume that you are trying to hide something; it is harder for employers to quickly determine your employment history. 3. Combination-includes features of both chronological and functional approaches. Advantages include: you can highlight both your skills and your employment history. Disadvantages: employers are somewhat unfamiliar with it, it can be repetitious and longer than other formats.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_054-->There are many considerations for the job seeker when thinking about preparing a résumé. Some of these include what type of résumé to prepare and how to handle the variety of unique circumstances that are present when dealing with different employers and positions. In this respect, why do most employers prefer chronological résumés over functional résumés? What kind of changes would you recommend that applicants make to their résumé if they are overqualified for the position they are applying for?

generalfeedback.text:
The functional résumé can obscure the applicant's work history and that is why many employment professionals are suspicious of it. Chronological résumés are easier to navigate and understand for employers.
Most organizations want to hire people who have the right qualifications, unless the applicant pool does not provide a quality hire. If one is an overqualified applicant, the applicant can still apply for the job because the person could be the right fit for the position. However, it is advisable to tone down one's résumé, focusing exclusively on the experience and skills that relate to the position. It would also help to highlight the applicant's knowledge of latest technology and processes that would be beneficial to the organization. Personal attributes such as leadership skills, organizational loyalty, and creativity could also be highlighted.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_055-->If you were fired from your previous job because of discrimination by your employer, should you include that work experience in your résumé? Why or why not?

generalfeedback.text: (Answers may vary.) The inclusion of that work experience depends on its relevance. If it was short-term and not significant, it's better to omit it. However, if it's important, you can include it and explain the circumstances of your dismissal to prospective employers during the interview process. Address their concerns with evidence, focusing on how the skills and knowledge gained in that position would benefit the organization.

Achievements and skills that are irrelevant to the position should be excluded. questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_098-->Describe the main sections or elements included on most résumés.

generalfeedback.text: 1. Name and address-any information necessary to contact you including phone numbers, e-mail addresses, etc. 2. Career Objective-this section is optional. Including it allows you to clearly state your desired goal and to categorize yourself. 3. Education-give your educational background, degrees earned, where you attended school, the dates attended, and the skills and abilities that you've developed in your course work. 4. Work Experience, Skills, and Accomplishments-list your jobs in chronological order with the current one first. Give the name and location of the employer as well as your title. Describe your skills and accomplishments and quantify them whenever possible. 5. Activities and Achievements-list volunteer activities that demonstrate your leadership, organization, teamwork, etc. Explain how the skills learned there are related to the job you're applying for. Note any awards you've received. 6. Personal data-like Career Objective, this section is optional. Include information about your interests and hobbies only if they enhance the employer's understanding of why you would be the best candidate for the job.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_099-->As someone who has just graduated, you may not have a clear career path when you enter the job market. How would your uncertainty affect the way your write your résumé? What is the purpose of the career objective section in a résumé and how does it serve the employer's needs?

generalfeedback.text:
(Answers may vary.) There is definitely uncertainty in writing a résumé when one doesn't have a clear career path. But instead of focusing on the lack of experience, I would focus on my qualifications and the best way to present them. By being organized and starting early, I can definitely get an edge in the process. Thinking like an employer and explaining how my general potential can serve the needs of the company is how I would choose to "sell" myself. This way the uncertainty of being inexperienced can be turned into positive energy which would help me create a persuasive, professional, and effective résumé.
A career objective identifies either a specific job you want to land or a general career track you would like to pursue. It is essentially about fulfilling your desires, not about meeting the employer's needs. But if it is worded in a way that relates your qualifications to employer needs, then it can generate attention.

answer.text: prepare a list of references and include them in their résumé
not prepare a list of references because in the United States she need not mention their names in her résumé
prepare a list of references only if she is applying for a position outside the United States
prepare a list of references but not necessarily include them in her résumé

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_008-->Kirndeep needs to immediately hire two copy editors for her organization. As with most companies that try to avoid the time and expense of sifting through thousands of applications, she decides to first …

answer.text: place an advertisement in the local newspaper, before going for the national newspapers
ask for recommendations from her employees
establish a presence at a local career fair
